content: 1. An intervention aimed at improving follow-up appointment adherence showed no significant effect. 2. A single study on socioeconomic support interventions demonstrated a reduction in mortality rates. 3. Two studies on community-based Directly Administered Antiretroviral Therapy (DAART) found no improvement in adherence. 4. A study examining the impact of community-based DAART on mortality found no significant effect. 5. However, one of the two studies on DAART showed an association with reduced mean viral load. 6. Another study on community-based DAART found no effect on retention in first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens. 7. Male sex, lower baseline CD4 cell count, and advanced WHO clinical stages (III and IV) were associated with higher mortality risk. 8. A retrospective cohort study in Rwanda reported a low mortality rate (5%) at two years post-ART initiation in a community-based ART program. 9. A non-randomized prospective cohort study in Uganda compared rural community-based ART programs with hospital-based programs, finding differences in treatment outcomes and mortality. 10. An observational study in Uganda reported that 86% of patients in a community-based ART program achieved viral suppression (<400 copies/mL). 11. Virologic failure was significantly associated with lack of CD4 response and prior antiretroviral use. 12. A South African study found that patients with community-based adherence support were more likely to maintain viral suppression (<400 copies/mL) at six months compared to those without such support. 13. Patients at sites with community-based adherence support services maintained viral suppression for longer periods than those at clinics without such services. 14. A study in South Africa reported high rates of virological suppression by 16 weeks post-ART initiation, with no significant variation across recruitment years. 15. Lack of virological suppression was associated with younger age (<25 years) and higher baseline viral load (>5 log10 copies/mL). 16. Adolescents (9–19 years) in a South African community-based ART program had significantly lower virological suppression rates at 48 weeks compared to young adults (20–28 years). 17. Adolescents also had a higher risk of virological failure than young adults, though this was not significant when limited to those perinatally infected. 18. A retrospective cohort study in Kenya found that participation in peer support groups and/or receiving home visits significantly prolonged time to treatment failure. 19. Patients in peer support groups had a significantly lower risk of treatment failure compared to those not in such groups. 20. A later report indicated that patients in rural community-based ART programs were more likely to achieve viral suppression at two years compared to those in hospital-based programs. 21. A South African study showed that patients with community-based adherence supporters had significantly higher treatment pickup rates (>95%) than those without such support. 22. A study in Mozambique reported that patients with a treatment partner had significantly higher adherence levels than those without a treatment partner. 23. No differences in adherence were observed between patients with community-based treatment partners and those with self-selected treatment partners. 24. A Kenyan study found that patients participating in support groups achieved higher mean adherence than those not in support groups. 25. A South African study reported significantly longer median retention in care for patients at sites with community-based adherence support services compared to those without such services. 26. Multivariate analysis showed that attrition was associated with older age (>50 years) and an interaction between baseline WHO clinical stage and sex. Men with advanced disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) were more likely to drop out of care than those with less advanced disease (WHO stage 1 or 2). 27. No studies were found evaluating the training of health workers providing care to adolescents living with HIV and its effect on adherence and retention. 28. One quasi-experimental study evaluated tools to enhance health workers' capacity to respond effectively and sensitively to adolescent clients. 29. Two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluated training of health workers caring for adolescents with other chronic conditions, assessing its impact on care quality and health outcomes. 30. An evaluation in Gujarat, India, found that training health-care providers using WHO adolescent health tools improved service quality and client experiences for young female clients (15–25 years). 31. Positive outcomes included better understanding of privacy needs, improved provider attitudes, adherence to recommended procedures, and enhanced client satisfaction. 32. An RCT on the Talking Diabetes intervention found no effect on HbA1c levels or self-reported adherence to diabetes medications. 33. The authors concluded that brief team-wide training in consultation skills may not improve glycemic control in children attending specialist diabetes clinics. 34. Another RCT involving children with asthma found that a planned care intervention significantly reduced asthma symptom days compared to standard care. 35. The planned care model was deemed effective for improving asthma care in primary care settings, while peer leader education alone was less comprehensive. 36. A survey and literature review on adolescents living with HIV (ALHIV) identified facilitators and barriers to accessing and remaining in care. 37. Most adolescents found accessing care and attending appointments easy or not challenging. 38. Barriers to access included cost, ARV stockouts, lack of trained health-care professionals, limited youth-friendly services, and stigma from providers. 39. Many adolescents had not discussed transitioning to adult services with their providers. 40. Most survey respondents reported positive interactions with health-care providers, with 85% rating their experiences as moderately to very good. 41. Respondents demonstrated high levels of autonomy in managing their health care, including seeking care, making appointments, and adhering to treatment. 42. Positive aspects of care included sensitive treatment by providers, home visits, peer group support, and interactions with optimistic providers. 43. Suggestions for improvement included age-appropriate support, material support, protection from stigma, comprehensive HIV education, and dedicated spaces for adolescents.
